title: "Rendering, post-processing and assembly"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
# A chunk's code sits under "Show code": open when it is what the page is
# about (`fold = "open"`), closed when it only supports it (`fold = "closed"`,
# the default unless the page sets another); `fold = FALSE` shows it plain,
# and so is code of three lines or fewer.
# Its results stay outside, always shown.
.fold_src <- knitr::knit_hooks$get("source")
knitr::knit_hooks$set(source = function(x, options) {
  f <- if (is.null(options$fold)) "closed" else options$fold
  # short code -- three lines or fewer, a chunk or the part of one before
  # its next output -- is shown as it is: folded, it would hide less than
  # the fold itself takes
  if (isFALSE(f) || length(unlist(strsplit(x, "\n", fixed = TRUE))) <= 3L) {
    return(.fold_src(x, options))
  }
  paste0("\n\n<details", if (identical(f, "open")) " open", ">",
         "<summary>Show code</summary>\n\n",
         .fold_src(x, options), "\n\n</details>\n\n")
})
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
                      message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
# The pictures of an assembled file are made by data-raw/gen_gallery.R (from
# the Gallery's outputs, through LibreOffice's PDF), committed in
# inst/rtf-examples/assemble/ and copied next to the article to be served.
.here <- normalizePath(".")
.shot <- function(file) {
  src <- file.path(.here, "..", "..", "inst", "rtf-examples", "assemble", file)
  if (!file.exists(src)) return(invisible(NULL))
  dir.create(file.path(.here, "figures", "assemble"), showWarnings = FALSE,
             recursive = TRUE)
  file.copy(src, file.path(.here, "figures", "assemble", file), overwrite = TRUE)
  knitr::include_graphics(file.path("figures", "assemble", file), error = FALSE)
}
```

```{r setup, fold = FALSE}
library(rtfreporter)
```

Once a document is built, three steps turn it into a deliverable: **render** it
to an `.rtf`, optionally **post-process** the file, and -- for a multi-table
package -- **assemble** several RTFs into one with a table of contents.

```{r doc}
df <- data.frame(
  Parameter = c("Creatinine clearance", "  Mean", "  SD"),
  Result    = c("", "88 ug/mL", "12 ug/mL"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
doc <- rtf_document() |>
  rtf_tables(as_rtftables(df), titles = list(c("Table 14.3.1 Renal Function")))
```


## Rendering -- `generate_rtfreport()`

`generate_rtfreport()` writes the document to a file you can open in Word or
LibreOffice. Use `overwrite = TRUE` to replace an existing file.

```{r render, fold = "open"}
out <- tempfile(fileext = ".rtf")
generate_rtfreport(doc, out, overwrite = TRUE)
file.exists(out)
```


## Post-processing -- `rtf_replace_text()`

Sometimes the rendered file needs a small tweak that you do not want to push
back into the (validated) source data. `rtf_replace_text()` does a find/replace
directly on the generated `.rtf`.

A typical case is **units**: the analysis dataset carries an ASCII-safe token
like `ug/mL`, but the report should display `µg/mL`. Rather than putting a
non-ASCII character in the data, render with the ASCII token and swap it in the
finished file. The replacement is the RTF unicode escape for `µ`
(U+00B5 = 181), i.e. `\u181?`:

```{r postprocess, fold = "open"}
final <- tempfile(fileext = ".rtf")
rtf_replace_text(out, "ug/mL", "\\u181?g/mL", output_file = final)

rtf <- paste(readLines(final, warn = FALSE), collapse = "\n")
grepl("\\u181?g/mL", rtf, fixed = TRUE)   # Word/LibreOffice show "µg/mL"
```

The same approach swaps any ASCII placeholder for a symbol you cannot (or
prefer not to) carry in the source data. `rtf_replace_text()` also supports vectorised
targets, fixed or regex matching (`use_regex = TRUE`), case-insensitive
matching, in-place editing (with an automatic `.bak`) or writing to a separate
`output_file`. See `?rtf_replace_text`.

> Note: rtfreporter already escapes non-ASCII characters you put in the data
> (so `"µg/mL"` in a cell renders correctly too). Post-processing is the tool
> for the "last mile" -- when the source must stay ASCII, or for a one-off fix
> to a finished file.


## Assembling several RTFs -- `assemble_rtf()`

A clinical deliverable is usually many tables, listings and figures. Render each
to its own `.rtf`, then combine them into a single document with a table of
contents using `assemble_rtf()`.

```{r make-files}
make <- function(title, path) {
  d <- data.frame(A = c("1", "2"), B = c("x", "y"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  doc <- rtf_document() |> rtf_tables(as_rtftables(d), titles = list(c(title)))
  generate_rtfreport(doc, path, overwrite = TRUE); path
}
f1 <- make("Table 14.1.1 Demographics",   tempfile(fileext = ".rtf"))
f2 <- make("Table 14.2.1 Adverse Events",  tempfile(fileext = ".rtf"))
```

### Automatic TOC

`toc = "auto"` builds one TOC entry per file, taking each label from the file's
first title:

```{r assemble-auto, fold = "open"}
pkg <- tempfile(fileext = ".rtf")
assemble_rtf(c(f1, f2), pkg, toc = "auto", overwrite = TRUE)
file.exists(pkg)
```

### Manual, multi-level TOC

For sections and explicit labels, pass the table of contents as a table: one
row per file, its `label`, and a `heading` printed above the entry whenever it
changes (`level` sets the indent). Each entry creates an RTF
**bookmark**, so the TOC is navigable in the word processor and the entries jump
to the right table:

```{r assemble-manual, fold = "open"}
pkg2 <- tempfile(fileext = ".rtf")
assemble_rtf(
  c(f1, f2), pkg2,
  cover = list(title = "Study XYZ-001", subtitle = "Final Tables", version = "v1.0"),
  toc = data.frame(
    file    = c(f1, f2),
    heading = c("EFFICACY ANALYSES", "SAFETY ANALYSES"),
    label   = c("Table 14.1.1 Demographics", "Table 14.2.1 Adverse Events")
  ),
  toc_page_numbering = "roman",
  overwrite = TRUE
)
file.exists(pkg2)
```

`assemble_rtf()` also takes a `cover` page and `toc_leader` / `toc_page_numbering`
options; see `?assemble_rtf`.

### Assembling a folder

To combine every RTF in a directory, `assemble_folder(dir, output_file)` reads
each file's table number and title into a table of contents and assembles them.
Without `output_file` it returns that table instead: edit the order, headings
and labels (or save it with `spec_file =` and edit it in Excel), then pass it
-- or its path -- to `assemble_rtf(toc = )`. See `?assemble_folder`.

### What the result looks like

The Gallery's demographics, adverse events, vital signs and listing, assembled
into one file with a cover page and a table of contents, then converted to PDF
with LibreOffice:

```{r shot-asm-toc, echo = FALSE, fig.alt = "The cover page (Study XYZ-001, Tables and Listings, Draft 1) and the table of contents, with headings and one entry per output; the adverse events entry is boxed in red, with a note that clicking it opens the AE table at page 4 of the PDF."}
.shot("toc.png")
```

Each entry of the table of contents is a link. Click the adverse events entry
and the reader opens that table's first page:

```{r shot-asm-target, echo = FALSE, fig.alt = "Page 4 of the PDF: the first page of Table 14.3.1.1, Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events by SOC and PT."}
.shot("target.png")
```

<details><summary>Show code</summary>

```r
files <- c("t_dm.rtf", "t_ae.rtf", "t_vs.rtf", "l_sae.rtf")   # the Gallery's outputs
assemble_rtf(
  files, "XYZ-001_tables.rtf", overwrite = TRUE,
  cover = list(title = "Study XYZ-001", subtitle = "Tables and Listings",
               version = "Draft 1"),
  toc = data.frame(
    file    = files,
    heading = c("DEMOGRAPHICS", "SAFETY", "SAFETY", "LISTINGS"),
    label   = c("Table 14.1.1  Demographic Characteristics",
                "Table 14.3.1.1  Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events by SOC and PT",
                "Table 14.3.5.1  Vital Signs by Visit",
                "Listing 16.2.7.2  Severe Treatment-Emergent Adverse Events")),
  toc_page_numbering = "roman")
system2("soffice", c("--headless", "--convert-to", "pdf", "XYZ-001_tables.rtf"))
```

</details>

### Bookmarks in the PDF

The assembled file is RTF. Each table of contents entry is a link to a
bookmark at the start of its file, and each file also starts with a heading
at an outline level, printed invisibly (white, one point high). Word and
LibreOffice show those headings as the PDF's bookmarks when they export the
file to PDF, so the PDF can be navigated table by table, as an eCTD
submission expects. With LibreOffice from R:

```r
system2("soffice", c("--headless", "--convert-to", "pdf", pkg2))
pdftools::pdf_toc(sub("[.]rtf$", ".pdf", pkg2))   # one bookmark a file
```

The page numbers in the table of contents are fields that already hold the
page rtfreporter computed for each file; Word and LibreOffice update them
when they refresh fields. The links and the bookmarks above were checked in
the PDF that LibreOffice writes. In Word itself a link follows on Ctrl+click,
its default setting.

That completes the basic workflow: build a document, render it, post-process if
needed, and assemble a package. See `?generate_rtfreport`, `?rtf_replace_text`,
and `?assemble_rtf` for full references.
